title: EU opens bidding for seven AI Gigafactories with €10 billion in public funding
subtitle: The European Commission's call targets €30 billion in total investment once private capital lands, with each large site hosting at least 100,000 AI chips and a November 12 application deadline.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: The European Commission on July 30 formally opened the call for proposals under its AI Gigafactories programme. Companies and consortia have until November 12, 2026, to bid to build up to seven facilities across the bloc, backed by €10 billion in public funding and targeting €30 billion once private co-investment is factored in. Award decisions are expected in early 2027. Three of the seven planned sites are large-scale, each equipped with at least 100,000 AI chips — roughly four times the compute density of a typical current European data center. Four smaller sites will host at least 75,000 chips each and can access up to €500 million in public funding.

The programme is Europe's most concrete attempt yet to close the compute gap with the US and China, and the mechanism it uses is unusual. Rather than subsidizing a single national champion, the Commission is putting public money behind operator-neutral shared infrastructure that startups, universities, industrial firms, and public agencies can all rent time on. This is closer to how the EuroHPC supercomputer network was structured than to the direct subsidies that supported chipmaking under the EU Chips Act.

The context is that Amazon, Microsoft, Google, and Meta are collectively spending over $600 billion on AI infrastructure in 2026 alone, and the largest of those single-site build-outs — Meta's Hyperion campus in Louisiana, OpenAI's Camellia complex in Georgia — exceed a full gigawatt each. Europe's seven Gigafactories, even at full private funding, would add roughly the compute of two or three US hyperscaler sites. The bet is not to match American capex, but to build enough sovereign capacity that European frontier work — Mistral, Aleph Alpha, Domyn, and the Anthropic-Microsoft sovereign-AI joint work in the region — can train without depending on US or Asian infrastructure.

For learners: the sovereignty story is worth understanding on its own terms, but the practical question for anyone building on European infrastructure is when this compute becomes rentable. November 2026 is the application deadline, early 2027 the award decision, and typical data-center construction runs 18 to 30 months after that. If you are planning European AI work that would benefit from local, non-hyperscaler compute, the answer is 2028 at the earliest — and probably 2029 for the large sites. Plan around that timeline, not the headline number.
